anime-taxonomy: A way to browse anime by who it was marketed to, what happens in it, where it takes place and how it looks. A title can belong to several branches at once.
action-features: The kinds of action you will see on screen, such as sword duels, gun battles or heroes transforming before a fight. These describe scenes rather than the whole story.
adaptation-source: The material an anime turns into animation: for example a manga, novel or game. This tells you where its story came from, not what genre it is.
audience-demographic: The audience a source work or publication was originally marketed to. These labels are not genres or age ratings.
character-trope: Recurring kinds of characters in anime, such as magical girls, idols or giant robots with personalities. These describe the cast rather than the intended audience.
cross-media-provenance: Connections between an anime and other media, such as comics, novels or live-action hero shows. Some labels describe the source story; others describe an influence.
distribution-formats: How an anime was first released: in weekly television episodes, as a cinema film, directly to home video or online. Later streaming availability can be different.
era-historical: The period portrayed in the story, such as feudal Japan or the Second World War. A historical setting can still include invented characters or magic.
format-production: How the anime is made and presented, from a television series to a short film, and from hand-drawn images to computer animation.
industry-fandom: Labels about animation as an industry or hobby, such as original productions, awards and fan culture. They do not promise a particular plot or quality.
narrative-genre: The main kind of story you can expect, such as an adventure, mystery or romance. Anime often combines several of these.
place-setting: The surroundings where events happen, such as a school, a city or outer space. This describes the location, not necessarily the main activity.
production-styles: How the anime looks or tells its story visually, such as tiny chibi character designs, black-and-white imagery or deliberately experimental scenes.
production-techniques: How the moving images are created, such as drawing characters, rendering 3D models or photographing physical models one frame at a time.
romance-types: How romantic relationships are arranged or developed: for example competing love interests, a love triangle or attraction that remains unspoken.
setting: The world and surroundings of the story. It can describe a place, a time period or a situation such as school or working life.
situational-setting: The shared situation that brings characters together, such as a school club, workplace or military academy. It can shape their daily routines and conflicts.
sports-types: The particular sport the characters practice or compete in. Training, rivalries, teamwork and matches often drive these anime.
structure-story-pattern: The way events are arranged across episodes, such as a new monster each week, a tournament or a character beginning a new life in another world.
subject-theme: What the anime spends time exploring, such as music, friendship at work, war or gaming. The same subject can appear in a comedy, drama or action story.
temporal-setting: When the story takes place, from prehistoric times to imagined futures. This is separate from the year the anime was released.
tone-mood: The feeling an anime aims to create, such as comfort, dread, laughter or suspense. Two shows about the same subject can have very different moods.
abstract: Uses nonliteral imagery or ideas, often putting visual expression ahead of a conventional plot.
absurd: Uses deliberately illogical situations or surreal humor that disregard everyday expectations.
action: Features physical conflict, chases or other fast-moving confrontations.
adventure: Follows journeys, exploration or quests into unfamiliar situations.
age-gap: Features a relationship where a substantial age difference is relevant to the story.
avant-garde: Experiments with conventional storytelling, visuals or presentation.
biography: Depicts the life of a real person, sometimes with dramatized events.
coming-of-age: Follows personal growth and the transition toward greater maturity or independence.
conspiracy: Involves concealed plans by groups or institutions and efforts to uncover them.
contemporary-fantasy: Places magical or fantastic elements in a broadly modern-day world.
dark-comedy: Uses disturbing, tragic or taboo situations as material for humor.
drama: Emphasizes emotional conflict, relationships and consequential personal choices.
gag-humor: Builds comedy around frequent jokes or short comic situations, sometimes with little ongoing plot.
harem-reverse-harem: An umbrella for stories in which several potential romantic partners surround one central character.
high-stakes-game: Games or contests have serious consequences, such as survival, freedom or major losses.
love-polygon: An interconnected romantic situation involving several people with overlapping attractions.
love-status-quo: Romantic tension persists while the central relationship situation changes little.
love-triangle: Three characters are connected by competing or overlapping romantic interests.
mind-twisting: Uses puzzling structures, shifting perspectives or revelations that challenge the viewer's interpretation.
mystery: Centers on unanswered questions and the discovery of hidden information.
reverse-harem: Usually features a female lead surrounded by several male potential romantic partners.
romantic-comedy: Combines developing romantic relationships with comic situations.
romantic-subtext: Suggests romantic attraction without making it an explicit or central relationship.
satire: Uses humor, exaggeration or irony to criticize behavior, institutions or social conventions.
school-life: Focuses on students' everyday experiences, friendships and activities at school.
sentai: A team of costumed or powered heroes who fight together, often with different colors, roles and coordinated attacks. Anime can borrow this pattern from Japanese live-action hero shows.
slapstick: Physical comedy built around exaggerated mishaps, movement and comic impacts.
slow-life: Emphasizes a less hurried lifestyle, routines and everyday satisfactions.
sudden-girlfriend-appearance: A potential romantic partner unexpectedly enters the protagonist's life, setting the plot in motion.
survival: Characters struggle to stay alive against dangerous circumstances or limited resources.
urban-fantasy: Combines city life with magic, supernatural beings or hidden fantastic worlds.
abuse: Depicts physical, emotional or other mistreatment as a story topic. The label does not indicate approval.
amnesia: Memory loss affects a character's identity, relationships or understanding of events.
archery: Characters practice shooting arrows at targets, often through Japanese kyudo clubs or competitive training. Technique, concentration and team pressure can drive the story.
arts: Explores artistic creation, practice or appreciation.
baseball: Characters train and compete in the bat-and-ball team sport, often aiming for a school championship. Pitcher–batter rivalries and team growth are common story threads.
boxing: Characters train to fight with punches inside a ring under sporting rules. Footwork, stamina, weight divisions and rival matches can shape their progress.
bullying: Explores repeated intimidation, exclusion or harassment and its effects.
childcare: Features caring for children and the responsibilities or relationships involved.
club: School clubs or other organized interest groups are important to the characters' activities.
combat-sports: Features organized sports based on physical combat, such as boxing or wrestling.
cooking: Preparing food and developing cooking skills are important activities.
crime: Features criminal acts, their consequences or the people involved in them.
cycling: Characters ride bicycles for competition, travel or a shared hobby. Racing anime may emphasize endurance, pacing and teammates taking different roles.
dancing: Dance practice, performance or competition plays a significant role.
educational: Aims to teach factual information or practical concepts through its presentation.
erotica: Stories where sexual attraction and erotic situations are a substantial focus. Catalogs differ in how explicit this label is, so consult the individual title’s content rating.
fishing: Features catching fish as a hobby, livelihood or competitive activity.
gambling: Characters wager money or other valuables on uncertain outcomes.
game: Games and their rules, players or competitions are important to the story.
genetic-modification: Features deliberate changes to genes or inherited biological traits.
gore: Includes graphic depictions of bodily injury or bloodshed.
gourmet: Focuses on enjoying, evaluating or exploring food and dining.
gymnastics: Characters train for controlled acrobatic routines, on apparatus or in rhythmic performance. Stories often focus on precision, practice and competition pressure.
human-enhancement: Explores technologies or interventions that extend human abilities.
ice-skating: Characters perform or compete on ice skates. In figure-skating stories, choreography, jumps, music and performance pressure often matter as much as the competition.
livestreamers: Features people who broadcast live content to an online audience.
mmorpg: Features massively multiplayer online role-playing games or worlds modeled on them.
magic: Supernatural techniques, spells or magical forces are part of the story.
martial-arts: Features established or fictional combat disciplines and their practice.
medical: Medicine, healthcare or the work of medical professionals is important to the story.
music: Music-making, performers or musical activities are important to the work.
mythology: Draws on traditional stories about gods, heroes or supernatural origins.
natural-disaster: Natural catastrophes and their effects are important to the story.
organized-crime: Features criminal organizations and their coordinated activities.
otaku-culture: Explores dedicated fans of anime, manga, games and related hobbies. Stories may involve conventions, collecting, cosplay, fan creations or the friendships and misunderstandings around those interests.
performing-arts: Features arts performed before an audience, such as theater, dance or music.
pets: Companion animals and their relationships with people are important to the story.
politics: Power, governance and political conflict shape the story.
racing: Features speed-based competition between people, vehicles or other racers.
seishun: Japanese for “youth.” Focuses on growing up through friendships, first love, school activities and hopes for the future, often with a bittersweet feeling about that time of life.
sexual-content: Indicates sexual material or themes. It does not by itself specify an age rating or degree of explicitness.
showbiz: Features the entertainment industry and the people working in it.
soccer: Teams try to score by moving a ball into the opposing goal, mainly with their feet. Anime often builds drama around formations, individual techniques and trusting teammates.
strategy-game: Games involving planning, tactics and consequential decisions are important to the story.
supernatural: Features beings or events beyond ordinary natural explanations.
superpowers: Characters possess extraordinary abilities beyond normal human capabilities.
swimming: Characters train or compete in the water, with different strokes and individual or relay events. Improving times and learning to rely on teammates are common story concerns.
team-sports: Features sports played by cooperating teams.
tennis: Features tennis players, training or competition.
terrorism: Features politically or ideologically motivated attacks intended to intimidate a wider population.
time-travel: Characters or information move between different points in time.
tournaments: A structured series of competitive matches organizes part of the story.
vtubers: Features performers who use virtual avatars for online videos or live broadcasts.
vehicles: Vehicles and their use, design or operation are important to the work.
video-game: Features video games, gaming or worlds associated with them; this alone does not mean an adaptation.
violent-content: Indicates physical violence. Frequency and graphic detail depend on the individual title.
virtual-reality: Features simulated environments experienced through immersive technology.
visual-arts: Features image-making arts such as painting, drawing, sculpture or photography.
voice-acting: Features performing voices for animation, games or other media.
volleyball: Two teams send a ball over a net using passes, sets, blocks and spikes. Anime commonly follows how players with different strengths learn to coordinate.
work-life: Focuses on working life, occupations and relationships around a workplace.
wrestling: Features wrestling as a sport or staged professional entertainment.
suspense: Builds tension by keeping viewers uncertain about a threat or outcome.
tragedy: Serious loss, suffering or downfall shapes the story's emotional direction.
adult-cast: Adult characters make up a significant part of the principal cast; this is not a content rating.
aliens: Features beings originating from beyond Earth.
androids: Features artificial beings designed to resemble humans.
angels: Features angelic beings, with interpretations that vary between fictional worlds.
anthropomorphic: Nonhuman beings or objects are given human traits, behavior or forms.
bishoujo: A design label for appealing female characters, often emphasizing polished faces, expressive eyes and carefully styled outfits. It describes character presentation rather than a specific plot.
bishounen: A design label for elegant or beautiful male characters, often with slender proportions, delicate features and carefully styled hair. It does not imply a particular romantic orientation.
combining-mecha: Several machines or parts join together to form a larger robot or machine.
crossdressing: Characters wear clothing associated with a different gender. This alone does not establish their gender identity.
cyborgs: Features beings that combine biological bodies with mechanical or electronic components.
delinquents: Features youths associated with rule-breaking, fighting or rebellious subcultures.
demons: Features demonic beings; their origins and morality vary by fictional setting.
detectives: Features investigators who uncover facts or solve cases.
dragons: Powerful reptile-like creatures, often able to fly or use supernatural abilities. Anime may portray them as enemies, companions, guardians or intelligent peoples.
elves: Fantasy peoples commonly drawn with pointed ears and associated with long lives or magic. Anime worlds vary in their culture, abilities and relationships with humans.
gangs: Features organized groups associated with street conflict, delinquency or crime.
ghosts: Features spirits of the dead or ghost-like apparitions.
gods: Features deities or divine beings as part of the story.
hero: A character who takes on danger or responsibility to protect others or achieve a larger goal. The label does not require superpowers or guarantee that the person is morally flawless.
heroine: A woman or girl in a leading or heroic role. She may lead an adventure, drive the romance or protect others; the label does not require a specific personality or power.
hunters: Features characters whose role involves tracking and pursuing creatures or targets.
hybrids: Features beings combining traits or ancestry from different species or kinds.
idols: Features entertainment personalities whose singing, performance and public image are important to their appeal.
idols-female: Women or girls work as idol performers, combining singing, dancing and a public persona. Stories can follow auditions, rehearsal, fan relationships and pressure to succeed.
idols-male: Men or boys work as idol performers, combining singing, dancing and a public persona. Stories can follow auditions, rehearsal, group rivalries and pressure to succeed.
kaijuu: Giant creatures whose size can threaten whole cities, often appearing in battles with humans, machines or other monsters. Their role can be destructive, protective or sympathetic.
magical-sex-shift: A supernatural or fantastic event changes a character's sex or bodily presentation; treatment varies by work.
maids: Characters who work as domestic attendants, or stories using maid-cafe and maid-costume conventions. Their duties and relationships may support comedy, romance or drama.
monsters: Nonhuman creatures that are strange, frightening or physically unusual. In anime they can be enemies, misunderstood neighbors or companions, not automatically evil.
ninja: Stealth-trained fighters associated with espionage, disguise and hidden techniques. Anime often expands these into supernatural abilities rather than historical realism.
pirates: Features maritime or fictional space pirates and their adventures.
police: Features law-enforcement officers and their work.
robots-mecha: Mechanical characters or machines play a noticeable role, from autonomous robots to human-piloted suits. Unlike the Mecha genre label, they do not need to be the main focus.
samurai: Warriors drawing on Japan’s historical sword-bearing military class. Stories often explore loyalty, duty, duels or life as a wandering swordsman, sometimes with fantasy additions.
sentient-mecha: Machines or robots possess their own awareness or personalities.
students: Student characters are important to the cast.
transforming-mecha: Machines change configuration or form, such as between a vehicle and a robot.
vampires: Beings associated with drinking blood, unusual longevity and supernatural powers. Anime may treat them as monsters, romantic figures or a distinct society.
witches: Characters who practice witchcraft, such as spells, potions or magical study. They may be students, helpers or threats depending on the anime’s world.
youkai: Supernatural beings from Japanese folklore, such as shape-changing foxes, tengu or strange household spirits. They may be frightening, mischievous or friendly; they are not all ghosts or villains.
zombies: Reanimated dead or infected beings portrayed as zombie-like threats. Stories may focus on survival and contagion, though some use the premise for comedy.
afterlife: A realm or existence after death forms part of the setting.
apocalypse: Catastrophic collapse or the end of the familiar world shapes the story.
art-school: A school specializing in visual or creative arts provides an important setting.
college: University or college life provides an important setting.
dystopia: An oppressive or deeply troubled society forms the setting.
historical: Set in an earlier historical period, with varying levels of factual accuracy.
martial-arts-school: A training institution for martial disciplines provides an important setting.
military-school: A military training institution provides an important setting.
music-school: A school specializing in musical training provides an important setting.
restaurants-stores: Restaurants, shops or their everyday operations provide important settings.
school: An educational institution is an important setting; the story need not focus on ordinary school life.
space: Outer space, space travel or off-world locations form an important setting.
steampunk: Imagines advanced machines built around steam engines, gears and the look of early industrial technology. Airships and mechanical cities are common, even when the world is entirely fictional.
western: Draws on frontier and Western-story conventions, often including outlaws, settlements or gunfighters.
feudal-japan: Uses a setting associated with Japan's feudal eras, sometimes with fantasy additions.
medieval: Uses a setting associated with the Middle Ages or a fictional world modeled on them.
prehistoric: Uses a setting before written history or a fictional interpretation of that period.
world-war-ii: Set during or substantially concerned with the Second World War.
cultivation: Characters train their body or spiritual energy to reach higher stages of power, often in Chinese fantasy animation. Breakthroughs, rival schools and the pursuit of immortality may shape the story.
episodic: Individual installments tell relatively self-contained stories, even when characters or larger arcs continue.
summoned-into-another-world: Characters are deliberately called into another world by a person or force within the story.
transported-into-a-novel: Characters enter a world identified with a novel or its story.
action-scenes: Contains sequences built around physical action; this does not necessarily make action the main genre.
black-and-white: Uses a predominantly monochrome visual presentation.
chibi: Uses small-bodied, oversized-head character proportions, for a whole work or selected scenes.
commercial: A short production made to advertise a product, service or organization.
dubbed: Presented with replacement voice performances in another language; availability depends on the release.
fan-service: Includes material intended to please an established audience, often suggestive imagery but sometimes references or spectacle.
flash-animation: Animation produced with the Flash workflow, often moving drawn shapes or reusable character parts. It can look flatter or more cutout-like than traditional frame-by-frame drawing.
henshin: Japanese for “transformation.” A character changes into a powered identity, often through a recurring sequence showing a new costume, armor or magical form.
movies: A film-format release, typically presented as a single feature rather than a series of episodes.
music-video: Animation made to accompany or promote a musical recording.
no-dialogue: Uses little or no spoken dialogue as a presentation choice.
picture-drama: Presents a story mainly through still illustrations with voices, music or limited movement.
power-suits: Features wearable suits that augment the wearer's strength, protection or abilities.
promotional: A production made primarily to promote another work, product or project.
proxy-battles: Characters compete through controlled creatures, machines or other representatives rather than fighting directly.
series: A production presented across multiple installments.
short: A short-duration production or short episodes; precise duration boundaries vary between sources.
special: A supplementary or standalone special release outside the main numbered series format.
stop-motion-animation: Animation made by photographing physical objects moved in small increments.
swordplay: Features combat or skill involving swords.
tv: Originally released as a television anime, usually in episodes.
tv-special: A special production released for television outside an ordinary episode run.
award-winning: Recognized by an award recorded in the source catalog; it is not a guarantee of personal enjoyment.
cartoon: A broad animation label that may refer to non-Japanese traditions or a strongly exaggerated drawing style. Its meaning depends on the source catalog, so it is less precise than the other branches.
comics: Stories told through sequences of illustrated panels and dialogue. This label can indicate a connection to comics; a source-specific adaptation label is more precise.
documentary: Presents factual subjects or real events, potentially using animation and dramatization.
foreign-anime: A catalog-dependent label for animation made outside Japan or involving other national animation traditions. It can include work marketed alongside anime; it is not a single visual style.
manga: Japanese comics, usually telling stories through drawn panels and dialogue. Here it describes a connection to that medium; “Based on Manga” specifically means the anime adapts one.
novel: A story primarily told through written prose. Here it indicates a connection to that medium; “Based on Novel” specifically identifies an anime adaptation.
original-work: The story was created for the anime instead of being adapted from an existing manga, novel or game. It can still later inspire books, comics or games.
parody: Imitates recognizable works or conventions for comic or critical effect.
tokusatsu: A connection to Japanese live-action effects traditions, including transforming heroes and giant monsters.
voice-actors: The performers who give animated characters their voices. This label may describe stories about that profession or a catalog’s focus on voice performers; it does not describe a genre by itself.
based-on-4-koma-manga: Adapted from four-panel comic strips, often built around a setup and punchline. The anime may join many short jokes into a continuous episode.
based-on-card-game: Adapted from a card game. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-comic-book: Adapted from a comic book. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-fairy-tale: Adapted from a fairy tale. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-light-novel: Adapted from a light novel, a prose-fiction publishing category often accompanied by illustrations. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-manga: The anime adapts a Japanese comic originally told through illustrated panels. It may compress chapters, change events or end before the comic does.
based-on-novel: Adapted from a prose novel. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-religious-text: Adapted from a religious text. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-song: Adapted from a song. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-video-game: Adapted from a video game. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-visual-novel: Adapted from a visual novel, an interactive story combining text and audiovisual presentation. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-web-novel: Adapted from a novel originally published online. The adaptation can change the original material.
based-on-webtoon: Adapted from a webtoon, a digitally published comic often designed for vertical scrolling. The adaptation can change the original material.
family: Anime made for children and adults to enjoy together, often with accessible adventures or everyday stories. Check the individual title’s content rating as well.
josei: An audience label for works originally marketed mainly to adult women, often through their source manga magazine. Stories can involve careers, relationships or other genres; it does not simply mean romance.
kodomo: Anime aimed mainly at children, often using straightforward stories, playful characters and easy-to-follow lessons. It is an audience label, not a guarantee that every scene suits every child.
seinen: An audience label for works originally marketed mainly to adult men, often through their source manga magazine. A seinen anime can be a quiet comedy as well as a serious thriller.
shoujo: An audience label for works originally marketed mainly to teenage girls. Romance and feelings are common, but magical adventures, comedy and other stories also fit.
shounen: An audience label for works originally marketed mainly to teenage boys. Training and rivalry are familiar patterns, but shounen also includes romance, comedy and other genres.
baihe: A Chinese storytelling label for romance or emotional relationships between women. In animation, it usually refers to the Chinese source material or tradition.
bara: A label often used outside Japan for male–male romance or erotic comics associated with gay male creators and readers. It is not interchangeable with all Boys’ Love, and its use varies by catalog.
boys-love: Also called BL: stories in which romantic relationships between male characters are a main focus. They may be gentle romances or more mature stories; the label alone does not specify explicit content.
cgdct: Short for “Cute Girls Doing Cute Things.” Usually follows a group of girls enjoying clubs, hobbies or daily routines, with friendship and small comic moments taking priority over major danger.
danmei: A Chinese fiction tradition focused on romantic or emotional relationships between male characters. Animated adaptations may present that relationship less directly than the source novel.
dark-fantasy: Fantasy strongly using disturbing, bleak, horrific, or psychologically dark subject matter.
gekiga-plot: Serious, dramatic storytelling influenced by gekiga, a Japanese comics tradition aimed at older readers. Expect human conflict and social concerns rather than a focus on broad cartoon jokes.
girls-love: Also called GL or yuri: stories centered on romantic or emotionally intimate relationships between female characters. The label alone does not specify explicit content.
mecha: Anime centered on giant robots or mechanized humanoid machines, piloted or autonomous.
real-robot: Giant robots are treated like equipment: pilots train, machines need maintenance and supplies, and tactics matter. They can still use fictional technology; “real” describes the storytelling approach.
romance: Stories with central romantic attraction, relationships or courtship arcs.
sekai-kei: Stories where a small number of characters’ feelings or relationships are directly tied to the fate of the world, with relatively little attention to governments or wider society.
slice-of-life: Stories emphasizing ordinary activities, routines, relationships and small-scale events.
super-robot: Giant robots are treated more like larger-than-life heroes, with spectacular signature attacks, unusual powers and dramatic transformations. The focus is often the pilot’s spirit and heroic battles.
workplace: Stories centrally concerned with work tasks, colleagues, and professional routines.
wuxia: Chinese martial-arts adventures about wandering fighters, rival schools and personal codes of honor. Fighters may perform extraordinary feats, but the focus is usually martial skill and human conflicts.
xianxia: Chinese fantasy about pursuing supernatural power or immortality through spiritual training. Characters may rise through levels of cultivation, encounter divine beings and travel between fantastic realms.
body-sharing-body-swapping-reincarnation: Groups stories where identity and the body no longer line up in the usual way: two minds share a body, people exchange bodies, or someone is born into a new life. The narrower labels distinguish these premises.
ecchi: Suggestive comedy or fan service, such as teasing situations and revealing imagery, without necessarily depicting explicit sex. The amount and age suitability vary by title.
hentai: A catalog label for sexually explicit animation intended for adults. It describes explicit content rather than a particular story genre.
military: Subject matter centered on armed forces, hierarchy, warfare preparedness or military life.
sports: Athletics and competition as a central narrative subject.
war: Organized armed conflict as a substantive story theme.
comedy: Stories centered on humor, jokes, playful conflicts, or comic setups.
horror: Stories designed around fear, dread, uncanny threat, and disturbing content.
iyashikei: Literally “healing-type”: quiet anime made to feel soothing, often through nature, gentle friendships and unhurried daily routines. Enjoying the atmosphere matters more than a tense plot.
noir: Crime stories with distrust, morally compromised characters and a sense that choices carry lasting costs. Shadowy visuals and weary investigators are common, but not required.
psychological: The story puts you inside characters’ fears, beliefs or distorted perceptions. Suspense may come from questioning what is real or why someone behaves as they do.
thriller: Stories centered on danger, uncertainty, high-stakes tension and suspense.
magic-idol-singers: Combines magical-girl stories with singing or idol performance. A heroine may transform into a performer or use magic as part of her stage identity.
mahou-shoujo: Japanese for “magical girl.” A heroine gains powers or a magical identity, often with a transformation scene, special outfit and companions. These anime range from cheerful adventures to darker stories.
villainess: Centers on a woman cast as the antagonist in a romance-game or fantasy story. She may know that role is supposed to lead to punishment and try to avoid that fate or rewrite her relationships.
cyberpunk: Science fiction combining advanced computers or body technology with inequality, corporate power or social breakdown. Cybernetic bodies, hacking and questions about identity are common.
fantasy: Works featuring impossible or magical worldbuilding, supernatural systems, or fantastical premises.
isekai: Stories in which characters travel to, are summoned into, are trapped in or are reborn into another world or reality.
magic-school: Stories centered on an institution where characters formally study magical arts.
post-apocalyptic: Set after a destructive world-shaping catastrophe, whether or not society is oppressive or dystopian.
school-club: Stories substantially organized around membership and activity in an extracurricular school club.
science-fantasy: Narrative setting deliberately blending technological/science-fiction conventions and fantastical or magical ones.
science-fiction: Speculative works built around science, technology, futuristic conditions or scientific extrapolation.
space-opera: Grand adventures across space, with starships, rival factions and conflicts affecting many worlds. Personal loyalties and dramatic battles usually matter more than detailed scientific realism.
monster-of-the-week: Mostly episodic episodes each featuring a separate antagonist or monster.
reincarnation: A character is reborn into a new body or life, without necessarily transferring between worlds.
reverse-isekai: Otherworldly characters come to Earth or another ordinary home world, reversing the common isekai direction.
trapped-in-a-video-game: Plot where characters are unable to leave a videogame-like environment.
cg-animation: Animation made with computer-generated models or imagery, especially 3D characters and environments. It may imitate hand-drawn anime or deliberately look three-dimensional.
gekiga-style: A visual approach influenced by dramatic Japanese comics: more realistic figures, strong shadows and serious expressions. It describes the artwork, not whether the story contains violence.
ona: Original Net Animation: animation initially released online.
ova: Original Video Animation: first-distributed primarily through home video rather than first-run television or theatrical release.
